doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: 'Guardian Angels' and the fado song 'Velho Anjo' with Ana Moura
summary: After his mother's death Ries wrote a song for Ana Moura; guitarist Jorge Fernando's lyrics matched his unspoken feeling. Most of his music is about a person or experience.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: but I wrote that song because it just was like, it just came out, I didn’t think actually, it really just came out. And that’s happened a number of times in my life where it’s just like I feel these things happen. In fact my mother died really tragically very quickly, and she used to talk about guardian angels. And so I wrote a song called “Guardian Angels” that came out on one of my records and then so she used to talk about this that my brother who died was like watching over me. So then I remember I did a lot of work with this fado singer Ana Moura, and it was just after my mother died I wrote this song and I didn’t have any lyrics to it, and I didn’t title it but I wanted to write this song for Ana because fado music is so powerful and so passionate and I really love it. So I wrote this song for the recording and her producer, the guy who plays guitar for her, Jorge Fernando, who is amazing, I sent it to them so that they could learn it and he goes, “Well can I put lyrics to this?” I said, “Well sure.” So I didn’t say anything about the song, what it was about or even my feeling, I just sent the song. He gets it and he starts writing lyrics. I get there, I flew to Lisbon, they had already recorded the guitar, the Portuguese guitar, they recorded her vocal. I was just there then and I was like wow, that’s really beautiful. What are the lyrics? And he said, “Well you know my feeling was I call this ‘Velho Anjo’ which is fallen angel. And I immediately got chills. And he said, “The lyrics are about an angel that’s dying slowly and the feathers are coming off the wings.” I’m getting chills thinking about it because — so you talk about what music does, not only to me but to like, that that person on the other side of the world felt something in the music with just the notes and the chords. That that translated to him and he put that into lyrics without me even saying a word, just the feeling — so it was like okay that exists so that is there with just in the notes, without any lyrics. He put the lyrics to it — I said you can’t imagine what you just did for me. Like that — even if I would have told you but so these feelings are there. We musicians, we can capture that.

I’ve often wondered, song titles can be obvious or is it possible to write a tune and say I don’t know what to call this. And the fact that you hadn’t titled it left that opening for him perhaps, or maybe he would have gone there anyway but it’s a great story.

It was the combination of my mother just dying and like you know that feeling of like, and then thinking how would this work with a fado singer, knowing she would just bring so much passion to the song. But that was it. But most of my music is written thinking about a person in my life or an experience that I’ve had and that I try not to get technical with my music in the sense like I’m going to do this slick thing. It’s more about like this particular feeling that I have. And almost none of them have lyrics.
